title: Dart SDK Configs
description: A practical reference for Dart's project configuration files: pubspec.yaml, analysis_options.yaml, and the other config files you'll run into in a typical Dart SDK project.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
## What "Dart SDK configs" covers

A Dart project (pure Dart, no Flutter) is typically driven by a handful of
plain-text config files sitting at the package root:

| File | Required? | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pubspec.yaml` | Yes | Package identity, dependencies, SDK constraints, executables. |
| `pubspec.lock` | Generated | Resolved, pinned dependency versions. Commit it for apps, usually commit it for packages too. |
| `analysis_options.yaml` | No (but recommended) | Linter rules, analyzer behavior, excluded paths. |
| `.dart_tool/` | Generated | Package config, build caches. Never edit by hand. |
| `.gitignore` | No (but recommended) | Keeps generated dirs like `.dart_tool/` and `build/` out of version control. |
| `.env` / `--define` | No | Not a Dart-native concept, but commonly used for config values. See the Environment Variables guide. |

This section walks through each file you'll actually hand-write:
`pubspec.yaml` and `analysis_options.yaml`. The generated ones
(`pubspec.lock`, `.dart_tool/package_config.json`) are covered in the API
Reference section for completeness, since you'll still want to know how to
read them even though you never edit them directly.

## Minimal project layout

```bash
my_package/
  bin/
    my_package.dart
  lib/
    my_package.dart
  test/
    my_package_test.dart
  pubspec.yaml
  analysis_options.yaml
  .gitignore
```

Continue to [Configuring pubspec.yaml](/dart-sdk-configs/configuring-pubspec-yaml/) to
start setting up a real project.
Getting Started.Configuring pubspec.yaml:
`pubspec.yaml` is the one file every Dart package must have. It sits at the
package root and declares who the package is, what Dart SDK it needs, and
what it depends on.

## Minimal pubspec.yaml

```yaml
name: my_package
description: A one-line description of what this package does.
version: 1.0.0
publish_to: none # remove this line if you intend to publish to pub.dev

environment:
  sdk: ^3.5.0

dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0

dev_dependencies:
  lints: ^4.0.0
  test: ^1.25.0
```

## Field-by-field

### `name`

Must be a valid Dart library identifier: lowercase, `snake_case`, no
hyphens, must start with a letter or underscore. This becomes the package's
import name, e.g. `package:my_package/my_package.dart`.

### `description`

A short (60-180 character) summary. Required if you plan to publish to
pub.dev — pub.dev will warn or refuse to score packages with a missing or
too-short description.

### `version`

Follows semantic versioning, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with an optional
pre-release/build suffix, e.g. `1.0.0-beta.1+3`. For an application that
you never publish, this is mostly informational, but tools like `dart run`
and CI pipelines may still read it.

### `publish_to`

Set to `none` for any package you don't intend to publish to pub.dev — this
is the single most common line missing from private/internal packages, and
forgetting it means `dart pub publish` will happily try to publish your
private code if ever run by mistake.

### `environment`

Declares the SDK version constraint:

```yaml
environment:
  sdk: ^3.5.0
```

`^3.5.0` means "`>=3.5.0 <4.0.0`" — any 3.x release at or above 3.5.0. Set
the lower bound to the oldest Dart SDK feature you actually use (e.g. if you
use a language feature introduced in 3.3, don't claim `^3.0.0`).

### `dependencies` vs `dev_dependencies`

- `dependencies` — needed at runtime by consumers of your package.
- `dev_dependencies` — only needed while developing this package itself:
  test runners, linters, build_runner, mocking libraries. These are *not*
  pulled in when another package depends on yours.

### `executables`

For packages that ship a CLI tool via `bin/`:

```yaml
executables:
  my_tool: my_package
```

This lets `dart pub global activate` expose `my_tool` as a runnable
command, mapped to `bin/my_package.dart`.

### `dependency_overrides`

Forces a specific version/source for a transitive dependency, overriding
whatever version constraints your direct dependencies asked for. Common
during local development against an unpublished branch:

```yaml
dependency_overrides:
  my_package:
    path: ../my_package
```

Never leave `dependency_overrides` in place for a published package unless
you mean it — it silently ignores your dependents' constraints.

See [Dependency Sources](/dart-sdk-configs/dependency-sources/) for git, path, and
hosted dependency syntax, and [pubspec.yaml Reference](/dart-sdk-configs/pubspec-yaml-reference/)
for the complete field list.
Getting Started.Configuring analysis_options.yaml:
`analysis_options.yaml` controls the Dart analyzer and linter: which lint
rules run, which errors are promoted/demoted in severity, and which paths
to ignore. It's optional — Dart works fine without one — but any project
beyond a quick script benefits from having one.

## Minimal setup using a lint package

The idiomatic starting point is to depend on a shared lint package and
`include` it, rather than hand-picking every rule:

```yaml
# pubspec.yaml
dev_dependencies:
  lints: ^4.0.0
```

```yaml
# analysis_options.yaml
include: package:lints/recommended.yaml
```

`package:lints` ships two presets:

- `package:lints/core.yaml` — the bare minimum, rules the Dart team
  considers correctness issues.
- `package:lints/recommended.yaml` — `core.yaml` plus a broader style/best
  practice set. This is what `dart create` scaffolds by default.

There's also `package:very_good_analysis` (community-maintained, much
stricter) if you want a stronger starting baseline than `lints` provides.

## Overriding individual rules

You can layer your own `linter:` block on top of an `include:`:

```yaml
include: package:lints/recommended.yaml

linter:
  rules:
    prefer_single_quotes: true
    avoid_print: false
    lines_longer_than_80_chars: false
```

`true` enables a rule, `false` disables it, even if the included preset
turned it on.

## Analyzer-level settings

Separate from lints, the `analyzer:` block controls the analyzer itself:

```yaml
analyzer:
  language:
    strict-casts: true
    strict-inference: true
    strict-raw-types: true
  errors:
    invalid_annotation_target: ignore
    todo: ignore
  exclude:
    - "build/**"
    - "lib/generated/**"
    - "**/*.g.dart"
```

- `language:` toggles stricter static-checking modes beyond null safety.
- `errors:` reclassifies specific diagnostic codes (`ignore`, `info`,
  `warning`, `error`).
- `exclude:` keeps generated or vendored code out of analysis entirely —
  essential once you introduce `build_runner`-generated `*.g.dart` files,
  otherwise the analyzer will flag lint violations in code you don't hand-edit.

## Where the analyzer looks

`analysis_options.yaml` must sit at the package root (next to `pubspec.yaml`)
to apply to that package. A monorepo with multiple packages needs one per
package, though a shared base file can be `include:`d from each:

```yaml
# packages/foo/analysis_options.yaml
include: ../../analysis_options.shared.yaml
```

See [Linter Rules Reference](/dart-sdk-configs/linter-rules-reference/) for commonly
toggled individual rules.

Guides.Setting Up a New Pure Dart Project:
A walkthrough of going from nothing to a properly configured pure-Dart
package on Arch Linux, using only `dart` (no Flutter tooling required).

## 1. Install the Dart SDK

On Arch Linux, the `dart` package is in the `extra` repo:

```bash
sudo pacman -S dart
dart --version
```

## 2. Scaffold the project

```bash
dart create -t package my_package
cd my_package
```

`dart create -t package` gives you `pubspec.yaml`, `analysis_options.yaml`
(already including `package:lints/recommended.yaml`), `lib/`, `test/`, and a
`.gitignore` pre-populated with `.dart_tool/` and other generated paths.

Other templates worth knowing:

```bash
dart create -t console my_cli     # a runnable CLI app (bin/ entrypoint)
dart create -t server-shelf my_api # a shelf-based HTTP server
```

## 3. Pin the SDK constraint deliberately

Open `pubspec.yaml` and check the `environment:` block matches the SDK you
actually have installed:

```bash
dart --version
# Dart SDK version: 3.9.0 (stable) ...
```

```yaml
environment:
  sdk: ^3.9.0
```

Don't just leave whatever `dart create` guessed — align it to your minimum
supported version intentionally.

## 4. Add dependencies

```bash
dart pub add http
dart pub add --dev test
```

`dart pub add` edits `pubspec.yaml` for you and immediately resolves +
writes `pubspec.lock`. Avoid hand-editing dependency versions and forgetting
to re-run `dart pub get` afterward — the lockfile won't update itself.

## 5. Verify

```bash
dart analyze
dart test
dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .
```

Run all three in CI (see [CI Setup with GitHub Actions](/dart-sdk-configs/ci-setup-with-github-actions/))
so config drift gets caught before merge.
Guides.Managing Dependency Versions:
How Dart's version constraints and lockfile actually behave, and the
commands you'll reach for day to day.

## Caret syntax

```yaml
dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
```

`^1.2.0` expands to `>=1.2.0 <2.0.0` — pub assumes semantic versioning, so
anything before the next major is considered compatible.

## Resolving vs upgrading

```bash
dart pub get      # resolve deps to satisfy pubspec.yaml, respecting pubspec.lock if present
dart pub upgrade   # re-resolve ignoring pubspec.lock, picking newest allowed versions
dart pub outdated  # report what's outdated, including majors blocked by your constraints
```

`dart pub get` is what you run after cloning a repo or editing `pubspec.yaml`
by hand — it's the safe, lockfile-respecting operation. `dart pub upgrade`
is what you run deliberately when you want to bump within your existing
constraints.

## Upgrading a single package

```bash
dart pub upgrade http
```

Re-resolves only that package (and anything it forces to move) to the
newest version still satisfying your constraint. To go past your
constraint intentionally:

```bash
dart pub add http:^2.0.0
```

## pubspec.lock

Generated by `dart pub get`/`upgrade`, and pins every resolved package to
an exact version + hash. For applications, always commit it — it's what
makes your build reproducible. For packages meant to be depended on by
others, committing it is still common practice (it doesn't affect what
your dependents resolve, since they ignore your lockfile, but it keeps
your own CI/tests reproducible).

## Dependency overrides for local development

Working on two packages together, before either is published:

```yaml
dependency_overrides:
  shared_models:
    path: ../shared_models
```

Remove before publishing — pub.dev will refuse to publish a package with
active `dependency_overrides` pointing at unpublished sources like `path:`
or `git:`.
Guides.Ignoring Generated Files with .gitignore:
`.gitignore` isn't Dart-specific, but every Dart project needs one tuned to
what the SDK generates. `dart create` scaffolds a reasonable default; this
page explains what's in it and why.

## Baseline .gitignore for a pure Dart package

```gitignore
# Files and directories created by pub.
.dart_tool/
.packages
build/

# Conventional directory for build/test artifacts.
.buildlog/

# Directory created by dartdoc.
doc/api/

# Avoid committing pub-generated files.
pubspec.lock
```

That last line is commented out or removed in most real-world
`.gitignore` files — see the note below.

## Line by line

- **`.dart_tool/`** — always ignore. Holds `package_config.json` and other
  machine-specific, fully regenerable state. Never commit it.
- **`.packages`** — legacy pre-Dart-2 package resolution file. Modern SDKs
  don't generate it by default, but old tooling or scripts might; ignore it
  if it appears.
- **`build/`** — output directory for `build_runner` and other build
  systems. Regenerable, ignore it.
- **`.buildlog/`** — used by some older build tooling for incremental build
  tracking. Safe to ignore if present.
- **`doc/api/`** — default output directory for `dart doc`. Regenerable
  HTML, don't commit it (publish it separately via GitHub Pages or
  pub.dev's hosted docs instead).

## Should pubspec.lock be ignored?

This is the one line worth deliberately deciding on rather than copying
blindly, and the guidance differs from the scaffold default:

- **Applications** (things you deploy — CLI tools, servers): do **not**
  ignore `pubspec.lock`. Commit it. You want the exact resolved versions
  reproduced on every machine and every CI run.
- **Packages published to pub.dev**: also commonly committed today, for
  the same local-reproducibility reason — see the FAQ entry on this in the
  [Project → FAQ](/dart-sdk-configs/faq/) page. It has no effect on what
  version your dependents resolve, since pub always ignores a dependency's
  own lockfile.

So in practice, most projects should remove or comment out the
`pubspec.lock` ignore line that some older scaffolds include.

## Extras worth adding

```gitignore
# IDE
.idea/
*.iml

# OS
.DS_Store

# Env files with secrets — see Environment Variables & Config
.env
.env.*.local
```

None of these are Dart-specific, but they round out a typical project
`.gitignore`.
Guides.CI Setup with GitHub Actions:
A minimal GitHub Actions workflow for a pure Dart package, checking format,
lints, and tests on every push.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/dart.yml
name: dart

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dart-lang/setup-dart@v1
        with:
          sdk: stable

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: dart pub get

      - name: Check formatting
        run: dart format --output=none --set-exit-if-changed .

      - name: Analyze
        run: dart analyze --fatal-infos

      - name: Run tests
        run: dart test
```

## Notes

- `dart-lang/setup-dart@v1` with `sdk: stable` tracks the latest stable
  release; pin an exact version (e.g. `sdk: 3.9.0`) if you need
  reproducible CI independent of new Dart releases.
- `--fatal-infos` makes `dart analyze` exit non-zero even for `info`-level
  lints, not just errors/warnings — without it, CI can pass with lint
  violations still present.
- `dart format --set-exit-if-changed` fails the job if any file isn't
  already formatted, without modifying files in place (good for CI;
  `dart format .` without that flag rewrites files, which you want locally
  but not in CI).
- Cache `~/.pub-cache` between runs on large repos to speed up `dart pub
  get`; for small packages it's rarely worth the added workflow
  complexity.

API Reference.pubspec.yaml Reference:
Complete list of top-level `pubspec.yaml` fields for a pure Dart package
(Flutter adds more, e.g. `flutter:`, not covered here).

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | Required. `snake_case`, must be a valid Dart identifier. |
| `description` | string | Required to publish. 60-180 chars recommended. |
| `version` | string | Semver. Omit for apps that never publish, though most tooling tolerates its absence. |
| `publish_to` | string | Set to `none` for unpublished packages. Omit (or set a custom pub server URL) otherwise. |
| `environment.sdk` | string | Required. Dart SDK constraint, e.g. `^3.5.0`. |
| `dependencies` | map | Runtime dependencies, pulled in transitively by consumers. |
| `dev_dependencies` | map | Dev-only dependencies (tests, linters, codegen). Not transitive. |
| `dependency_overrides` | map | Forces a version/source, overriding constraint resolution. Remove before publishing. |
| `executables` | map | Exposes `bin/*.dart` entrypoints as global commands via `dart pub global activate`. |
| `platforms` | map | Declares which platforms a package supports (e.g. `native`, `web`) — informational, used by pub.dev scoring. |
| `topics` | list | pub.dev discovery tags, e.g. `- http`, `- networking`. Publish-only. |
| `funding` | list | Links shown on the pub.dev package page (e.g. GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective). |
| `false_secrets` | list | Glob patterns pub.dev's secret-scanner should ignore when publishing. Rare. |
| `screenshots` | list | Package screenshots shown on pub.dev. |

## `dependencies` entry shapes

```yaml
dependencies:
  # hosted (pub.dev), simplest form
  http: ^1.2.0

  # hosted, explicit form
  http:
    hosted: https://pub.dev
    version: ^1.2.0

  # git
  my_lib:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/user/my_lib.git
      ref: main
      path: packages/my_lib # only if the package isn't at repo root

  # local path (monorepos, local development)
  shared_models:
    path: ../shared_models
```

See [Dependency Sources](/dart-sdk-configs/dependency-sources/) for details on each
source type.
API Reference.Dependency Sources:
Dart dependencies can come from three sources. All three can appear in the
same `pubspec.yaml`.

## Hosted (pub.dev or a private pub server)

```yaml
dependencies:
  http: ^1.2.0
```

Equivalent explicit form, needed for a private/self-hosted pub server:

```yaml
dependencies:
  internal_pkg:
    hosted: https://pub.mycompany.dev
    version: ^2.0.0
```

## Git

```yaml
dependencies:
  my_lib:
    git:
      url: https://github.com/user/my_lib.git
      ref: main          # branch, tag, or commit SHA; omit for default branch
      path: packages/lib # only needed if pubspec.yaml isn't at the repo root
```

Pinning `ref` to a commit SHA rather than a branch name gives you a
reproducible build without needing `pubspec.lock` to be the only thing
holding the version steady — useful if you ever regenerate the lockfile.

## Path

```yaml
dependencies:
  shared_models:
    path: ../shared_models
```

Points at a sibling package on local disk, resolved relative to the
`pubspec.yaml` that declares it. Common in monorepos, or paired with
`dependency_overrides` for temporary local development against an
unpublished dependency.

## Constraint syntax cheat sheet

| Syntax | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `^1.2.0` | `>=1.2.0 <2.0.0` |
| `>=1.2.0 <2.0.0` | Explicit range, equivalent to above |
| `any` | Any version — avoid in shared packages, fine for quick scripts |
| `1.2.0` | Exact version only — rarely what you want, blocks patch updates |
API Reference.Linter Rules Reference:
A selection of individually toggleable rules commonly adjusted on top of
`package:lints/recommended.yaml`, grouped by what they're for.

## Style preferences

```yaml
linter:
  rules:
    prefer_single_quotes: true
    prefer_const_constructors: true
    prefer_final_locals: true
    directives_ordering: true
    sort_child_properties_last: true
```

## Correctness-leaning

```yaml
linter:
  rules:
    avoid_print: true            # off by default in `recommended`; on in stricter presets
    always_declare_return_types: true
    avoid_returning_null_for_future: true
    cancel_subscriptions: true
    close_sinks: true
```

## Rules people commonly turn off

```yaml
linter:
  rules:
    lines_longer_than_80_chars: false
    public_member_api_docs: false   # demands doc comments on every public member; noisy for app code
    avoid_print: false              # fine for CLI tools whose whole job is printing
```

## Checking what a rule does

```bash
dart analyze --help
```

Or browse the canonical, always-current list rather than relying on a
static reference: `dart.dev` publishes the full rule catalog with examples
for each rule, since new rules are added and some are deprecated across
Dart SDK releases.

See [Configuring analysis_options.yaml](/dart-sdk-configs/configuring-analysis-optionsyaml/)
for `include:`, `analyzer:`, and `exclude:` usage.
API Reference.dart_test.yaml Reference:
`dart_test.yaml` configures the `test` package's runner: default platforms,
timeouts, tags, and concurrency. Optional — `dart test` works with sensible
defaults without one — but useful once a test suite grows.

## Location

Sits at the package root, next to `pubspec.yaml`. Requires a `dev_dependency`
on `test`:

```yaml
# pubspec.yaml
dev_dependencies:
  test: ^1.25.0
```

## Minimal example

```yaml
# dart_test.yaml
timeout: 30s
concurrency: 4

tags:
  integration:
    timeout: 2x # multiplies the default timeout for tests tagged 'integration'
```

## Common fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `timeout` | Default per-test timeout, e.g. `30s`, `2m`, or `none`. |
| `concurrency` | How many test files run in parallel. Defaults to the number of CPU cores. |
| `platforms` | Restrict which platforms tests run on by default, e.g. `[vm]`. |
| `tags` | Define named tags with their own overrides (timeout, platform-specific `skip`, etc.), applied to tests annotated `@Tags(['name'])`. |
| `exclude_tags` / `include_tags` | Filter which tagged tests run by default without passing `--tags`/`--exclude-tags` on the command line every time. |
| `reporter` | Default output format: `compact`, `expanded`, `json`, `github` (annotates PRs in GitHub Actions). |
| `test_on` | Platform selector restricting the whole suite, e.g. `test_on: vm`. |

## Tagging tests

```dart
// test/integration/api_test.dart
@Tags(['integration'])
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  test('hits the real API', () {
    // ...
  });
}
```

```yaml
# dart_test.yaml
tags:
  integration:
    timeout: 1m
```

Then run subsets from the command line:

```bash
dart test                        # everything
dart test --exclude-tags=integration  # skip slow/integration tests locally
dart test --tags=integration          # only integration tests, e.g. in a separate CI job
```

## Per-directory overrides

```yaml
presets:
  ci:
    concurrency: 1
    reporter: github
```

Activate a preset explicitly:

```bash
dart test --preset=ci
```

Useful for keeping one config file but behaving differently in CI vs local
runs, without duplicating flags across workflow files.
API Reference.build.yaml Reference:
`build.yaml` configures `build_runner` — the code-generation pipeline used
by packages like `json_serializable`, `freezed`, `built_value`, and
`source_gen`-based tools generally. Only relevant if your project actually
uses codegen; skip this if you don't have `build_runner` as a dependency.

## When you need it

If you're using an annotation-driven codegen package and only need its
defaults, you often don't need a `build.yaml` at all — the generator
package ships its own default builder config. You add one when you need to
change *how* generation runs: output paths, which files are included, or
combining multiple generators.

## Setup

```yaml
# pubspec.yaml
dev_dependencies:
  build_runner: ^2.4.0
  json_serializable: ^6.8.0

dependencies:
  json_annotation: ^4.9.0
```

## Minimal build.yaml

```yaml
targets:
  $default:
    builders:
      json_serializable:
        generate_for:
          - lib/models/**.dart
        options:
          explicit_to_json: true
```

- `targets: $default:` — the default build target (your own package).
- `builders:` — keyed by builder name (as exposed by the generator
  package), configuring which files it applies to and generator-specific
  `options:`.
- `generate_for:` — glob(s) restricting codegen to specific files/dirs,
  useful in large packages to avoid regenerating everything on every build.

## Running codegen

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
```

- `--delete-conflicting-outputs` skips the interactive "overwrite?" prompt
  for previously generated files — standard for CI and most local
  workflows.

```bash
dart run build_runner watch --delete-conflicting-outputs
```

Watches for file changes and regenerates incrementally — the usual choice
while actively iterating on annotated classes.

## Excluding generated output from analysis

Generated files (typically `*.g.dart`, `*.freezed.dart`) should be excluded
from lint/format, not hand-edited or reviewed line-by-line:

```yaml
# analysis_options.yaml
analyzer:
  exclude:
    - "**/*.g.dart"
    - "**/*.freezed.dart"
```

They should still be committed to version control for applications (so a
fresh clone builds without running codegen first), though some teams
instead run codegen as a CI/build step and gitignore generated files —
either approach is common; pick one and be consistent.
API Reference.Generated Files Reference:
Files Dart tooling generates and maintains for you. Useful to know how to
read them; you should never hand-edit them.

## pubspec.lock

Written by `dart pub get` / `dart pub upgrade`. Pins every resolved
dependency (direct and transitive) to an exact version and content hash.

```yaml
# pubspec.lock (excerpt)
packages:
  http:
    dependency: "direct main"
    description:
      name: http
      sha256: "..."
      url: "https://pub.dev"
    source: hosted
    version: "1.2.2"
sdks:
  dart: ">=3.5.0 <4.0.0"
```

- `dependency:` records whether it's `"direct main"`, `"direct dev"`, or
  `"transitive"`.
- Regenerated automatically whenever `pubspec.yaml` changes and you run
  `dart pub get`. Manually editing it is pointless — the next `pub get`
  can overwrite fields it considers stale, and it isn't validated against
  `pubspec.yaml` the way you'd expect a hand-edit to be respected.

## .dart_tool/package_config.json

Written by `dart pub get`. Maps every package name in your dependency graph
to a file-system location, and is what the Dart VM/analyzer actually
consults at run time and analysis time — `pubspec.lock` is for version
resolution, `package_config.json` is for "where is package X on disk".

```json
{
  "configVersion": 2,
  "packages": [
    {
      "name": "my_package",
      "rootUri": "../",
      "packageUri": "lib/"
    },
    {
      "name": "http",
      "rootUri": "file:///home/psdk/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/http-1.2.2",
      "packageUri": "lib/"
    }
  ],
  "generator": "pub",
  "generatedDate": "2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
}
```

Never commit `.dart_tool/` — it's machine- and path-specific
(`rootUri` entries point at absolute paths on your disk, e.g. your
pub-cache location under your own home directory). Every clone/CI run
regenerates it fresh from `pubspec.lock` via `dart pub get`.

## .packages (legacy, pre-Dart-2)

Older Dart tooling (roughly pre-2.0) used a flat `.packages` file instead of
`.dart_tool/package_config.json`:

```
# .packages (legacy format)
my_package:lib/
http:file:///home/psdk/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/http-1.2.2/lib/
```

One line per package, `name:file-uri-to-lib-dir`. Modern Dart SDKs
(`configVersion: 2` in `package_config.json`) don't generate this file by
default. You'll only encounter it working with a very old package or a
tool that hasn't been updated — if you see one referenced, treat it as
dead weight and make sure it's in `.gitignore` rather than trying to
maintain it by hand.

## package_config.json schema versions

`configVersion` in `package_config.json` has had two values historically:

- `1` — original format, predates Dart 2's package resolution changes.
- `2` — current format, adds `languageVersion` per package (drives which
  null-safety/language-feature set each dependency is analyzed under) and
  is what every current Dart SDK writes.

You'll never write this by hand — it's here so that if you ever inspect
`.dart_tool/package_config.json` during debugging (e.g. tracking down why
the wrong version of a path-dependency is being picked up), the fields
make sense.
API Reference.Global Pub Config & .pubignore:
Two things that live outside a single project's config but still shape how
`dart pub` behaves: machine-level pub settings, and what gets left out of a
published package.

## Global pub cache location

By default, `pub` caches downloaded packages under `~/.pub-cache` (on
Linux, including Arch). Override it with an environment variable:

```bash
export PUB_CACHE="$HOME/.local/share/pub-cache"
```

Useful if you want the cache on a different disk/partition, or want
per-project isolation in unusual CI setups. Most single-machine dev setups
never need to touch this.

## PUB_HOSTED_URL

Points `pub` at a different package server instead of pub.dev — used for
self-hosted/private pub servers:

```bash
export PUB_HOSTED_URL="https://pub.mycompany.dev"
```

Combine with per-dependency `hosted:` entries in `pubspec.yaml` (see
[Dependency Sources](/dart-sdk-configs/dependency-sources/)) when only some
dependencies come from the private server.

## Credentials

`dart pub publish` and access to private hosted packages use
`~/.config/dart/pub-credentials.json` (XDG-style path on Linux; older SDKs
used `~/.pub-cache/credentials.json`). Written automatically the first time
you `dart pub login` or publish — never hand-author it, and never commit it
anywhere; it holds an OAuth token.

```bash
dart pub login    # interactive browser-based auth flow
dart pub logout   # clears stored credentials
```

## .pubignore

Controls what's excluded from the tarball uploaded by `dart pub publish` —
separate from `.gitignore`, which controls what's excluded from version
control. If `.pubignore` is absent, pub falls back to respecting
`.gitignore` for the publish tarball.

```
# .pubignore
test/fixtures/large_sample_data/
doc/internal_notes.md
*.draft.md
```

Use `.pubignore` when something should be committed to git (so
collaborators/CI have it) but shouldn't ship in the published package —
large test fixtures, internal-only docs, example data files. Most projects
never need one; `.gitignore` alone is usually sufficient since anything
not in git isn't published either way.

## Checking what will actually be published

```bash
dart pub publish --dry-run
```

Lists every file that would be included in the tarball — the fastest way
to confirm `.pubignore`/`.gitignore` are doing what you expect before a
real publish.

Project.FAQ:
### Do I need analysis_options.yaml at all?

No — `dart analyze` works without one, using built-in defaults. You lose
the ability to enable a shared lint preset or exclude generated files, so
any project beyond a throwaway script benefits from adding one.

### Should I commit pubspec.lock?

For an application (something you deploy, not something others
`pub add`): yes, always. For a package published to pub.dev: also commonly
committed, since it keeps your own CI and local dev reproducible — your
dependents never read your lockfile regardless, so it doesn't affect them.

### Why does dart pub get keep changing pubspec.lock even though I didn't touch pubspec.yaml?

Usually one of: a dependency you depend on with a loose constraint (`any`,
or a wide caret range) published a new version and you ran
`dart pub upgrade` instead of `dart pub get`; or the lockfile was out of
sync with `pubspec.yaml` from an edit that wasn't followed by `pub get`
before committing.

### What's the difference between dart pub get and dart pub upgrade?

`dart pub get` resolves dependencies while respecting the existing
`pubspec.lock` as much as possible — it only changes things `pubspec.yaml`
now requires. `dart pub upgrade` ignores the current lockfile and
re-resolves everything to the newest versions your constraints allow.

### Can I have multiple analysis_options.yaml files in one repo?

Yes, one per package in a monorepo (each next to its own `pubspec.yaml`).
A nested one overrides/extends anything from a parent via `include:`, it
doesn't need to redeclare everything.

### My CI passes locally with dart analyze but fails in the pipeline — why?

Almost always `--fatal-infos` (or `--fatal-warnings`) being set in CI but
not locally, surfacing `info`-level lints that a plain local `dart analyze`
run doesn't fail on.
Project.Changelog:
This docs set tracks Dart SDK configuration conventions as of Dart 3.9.
Notable recent-ish changes worth knowing if you're coming from an older
Dart version:

## Dart 3.x

- `dart create` templates now default to including
  `package:lints/recommended.yaml` in scaffolded `analysis_options.yaml`
  files, rather than an empty file.
- `dart pub` subcommands (`get`, `upgrade`, `add`, `remove`, `outdated`)
  are the standard interface; older standalone `pub` command invocations
  from Dart 1.x/2.x docs are no longer the documented entrypoint.
- Sound null safety is the only supported mode — the legacy
  `environment: sdk: '>=2.12.0 <3.0.0'` transitional constraints you may
  still see in older packages are no longer relevant to write yourself.

## License

This documentation is provided as-is for reference. Verify field names and
defaults against the current `dart.dev` documentation for anything
version-sensitive, since analyzer/linter defaults do shift across SDK
releases.
